what: Every error caught in the R(3,10) lane, by whom and how, from the control room’s log, its notes and its gate ledger: ours and the models’ alike, never a person’s. The rows of box 3 were one line each while it was sealed; since 25 Nov 2026 they carry their words and sources. A correction of a correction is one row, never counted as a finding.

rows.what: A note said the verified checker cake_lpr was built only for x86; its final release ships an ARMv8 build, which ran on the Mac.
A field of the global scout’s results held |J|, the touched part of a neighbourhood, under the name of |T| = |J| + 1; the claim was the same.
rows.outcome: the track was asked to name the field so

rows.what: Round 2 of the control room’s log was first stamped 02:15 UTC; it was written about 01:40.
The pilot’s pinned CNF generator was changed after it was pinned, and the pinned bytes were not on disk.
rows.outcome: the pinned bytes restored beside the changed file; listed as a gap

mattered.title: A pinned file changed after pinning
mattered.line: The pilot’s CNF generator was edited after its hash was pinned. The pinned bytes were restored beside it and the gap was listed.

rows.what: A first report said nothing was running; a second benchmark was running on four workers.
The run’s script hashed one of its files and then appended the end time to it, so one listed hash is of the file’s earlier state.
rows.outcome: listed; the file without its last line has the listed hash

rows.whose: the plan and the prior-art scout (an agent)
rows.caught_by: the reveal draft (an agent, reading our own files against each other)
rows.what: Two of our files said the Lean bridge rests on a native_decide axiom; the proof as checked uses none, only the three standard axioms. Both were written before the kernel proof.
rows.outcome: the result note is the record

rows.how: reading the statement against the record
rows.what: The sealed text adds that Exoo’s 39-vertex graph attains the bound. Our record shows only that a 39-vertex graph attains it; that it is Exoo’s rests on the two tracks’ checks.
rows.outcome: the page says “the bound 39 is attained”

rows.what: Our pre-registration says it was written about 17:35 UTC; its timestamp receipt was submitted at 17:22 UTC.
rows.outcome: listed; the receipt is the time

rows.what: Our plan still listed the verified checker as not run on C35; the result note has it accepting both proofs. One check time was also given as 0.6 s in three files and 0.31 s in the result.
rows.outcome: the result note is the record

rows.what: Our files disagree on who first stated C35: the brief, the round files and the sealed statement give three different splits between the two model tracks.
rows.outcome: open: the credit is mine to give

rows.what: A registration’s header said a draft’s hash was “in the block below”; it is in a separate file.
A brief gave the report’s author a wrong first name. The report and its Zenodo record name him Zhiyang Chen.

rows.how: building and reading by our own route
rows.what: A report called one Lean theorem “every independence clause at levels 3, 4 and full depth”: it is one theorem with the level idle, and no clause of the CNF is in that Lean.
rows.outcome: listed in the reading; no theorem changed

rows.what: An agent called leanchecker --help, which has no such flag and starts a full replay; stopped after about two minutes, nothing written. It happened again at 18:25 UTC.
rows.outcome: stopped; every later tool ran under a wrapper with limits

rows.what: The same slip as in production, this time in our script: it appended to a progress log after hashing it.
The first five replays exited 1 within a second: the tool started Lean from a path with no default toolchain.
rows.outcome: rerun with the toolchain first on the path; the failed logs kept

rows.what: A report cited a Lean line for the independence proof that holds another definition.
A note said three native runs passed; no log, script or binary of them is in its folder. The control room reproduced them.

mattered.title: Three runs with no files
mattered.line: A model’s note said three runs had passed; no log, script or binary was in its folder. The control room ran them again itself.

rows.what: A report’s list of what the production argument still needs was short by five items; its own note had two of them.
A report said a planted change was “caught at the first changed index”; the replay log holds no such control.

rows.how: an audit of the tightened pruning rule
rows.what: In the proof of the tightened pruning rule of the three-edge branch, one step was worded ambiguously. The step was valid: on 2,094 real graphs with the exact bound and 104,700 weight vectors the rule rejected no real graph’s own side triple.

rows.how: an audit of the blind pilot on 16 catalogue cores
rows.what: The pilot was presented as blind in time, its rules fixed before the draw. Only local clocks backed it: no OpenTimestamps receipt, no commit. File birth times and the session log agreed on the order, but neither is outside the Mac.

rows.how: an audit of the second pilot (four fresh cores)
rows.what: A second claim of registration before any outcome, again backed only by local clocks (no receipt).
The second pilot’s “separate verifier” was the same track’s code, written three minutes later.
The rented machine of the all-rows byte check stood idle 20 minutes after the run ended, because a notice arrived late: about US$0.32.
rows.outcome: deleted; pods are now checked near their expected end

rows.what: Our estimate for the full three-edge run was 9 to 11 hours and about US$10. After 115 cores it measured 125 s of wall per core, a projection of 15 to 25 hours; the run took about 961 CPU-hours on two machines in the end.
rows.outcome: recorded as a deviation; the operator chose to let it run

rows.how: an audit of the corrected records
rows.what: Four audited record files of the two pilots were corrected in place. The originals were kept under as-run/ with the audited hashes, but the two registrations’ bodies were edited, so their FROZEN.sha256 no longer checked and FREEZE.txt named a hash the file no longer had.
rows.outcome: restored at the audited hashes (19:29 UTC)

rows.what: The three-edge formula of the Hall screen, carried into the four-edge branch, is wrong there on 252 patterns of 4,096.
rows.outcome: replaced by the four-edge closed form, which brute force confirms on 4,096 of 4,096

rows.how: reading the report against its folder
rows.what: A report gave figures for its development core 0 (863,744 records; two sent to the fill search) with no file behind them.
rows.outcome: the files were produced later (20:39 UTC)

rows.what: A safeguard was claimed for future draws: “a draw cannot start without an outside receipt”. The program checked the receipt against FREEZE.txt’s bytes, never opened FROZEN.sha256, and the draw program asked for no receipt.
rows.outcome: refused; rebuilt and certified by reading (22:06 UTC)

rows.what: A note said 39 native rows matched the ledger’s hashes; its log held the word SAME and no hashes.
rows.outcome: the track added the 39 hashes (19:12 UTC)

rows.how: the track’s reply, then the files
rows.what: We wrote that no theorem joins the CNF’s soundness proof (T1) to the other track’s closing theorem. Wrong: its bridge applies T1, and the closing theorem’s hypothesis is written with the same constants. It repeated a gap that file had closed.

mattered.title: A gap that was not there
mattered.line: We wrote that no theorem joined the two halves of the R(7) Lean chain. The Claude track showed the join; we withdrew the claim and filed an erratum.

rows.whose: a model session (by its content, the Astra track’s)
rows.what: A session of the other track wrote into two of the Claude track’s result notes, under that track’s heading; it happened again at 19:32 UTC.
rows.outcome: the blocks moved out verbatim to a dated file; a rule: each track writes only in its own folders

rows.how: an audit of the four-edge work
rows.what: Four phrases in the Claude track’s four-edge note said more than its files: “both tests assume…”, “16 agree” (14 before, 2 after), “none at k = 5”, and “before the other file was opened”.

Audited files were replaced in place again: the three-edge reduction’s .tex and .pdf (19:06:07 UTC; the page our first note hashed no longer resolved at its path, and our reader rebuilt it byte for byte) and the four-edge reduction note. A hash list went stale on 10 of 61 lines.
rows.outcome: a rule: an audited file is never overwritten; a new version takes a new name

rows.what: A hash given in a message was taken before the file’s last write.
rows.outcome: checked against the file on disk

rows.what: A report said a fresh replay (leanchecker --fresh) had passed; its log had no such line. A transcript was filed later, without a time.

rows.how: an audit of the draw gate
rows.what: A test receipt shown as the track’s own, a “genuine receipt at block 974704”, was our first seal’s receipt, read in place from our seal folder.
An agent of ours ran two read-only git commands on our seal folder and left one empty file in the session’s scratch folder.

rows.how: an audit of draw gate v4
rows.what: Three hash suffixes were misprinted in our audit notes (…2d94 for …2fb2, …5d94 for …2d94, …632e for …023a); the files were right.
Our first draft of a public status line named this private lane’s rented machine. The commit was refused before it was made.
rows.outcome: rewritten with the public lane only

rows.how: an audit of the toy draws
rows.what: Both draw gates sent the User-Agent “cert-machine/round21” to the two block services, naming the project from a private lane.

rows.how: an audit of the second counting program
rows.what: A run presented as on an independent machine, “Debian 12 arm64”, was a virtual machine on the same Mac.

rows.how: an audit of the Claude track’s note
rows.what: Two statements in the Claude track’s note were refuted (that the pigeon test can fire on a Hall survivor; a gap claimed as a catalogue fact), and a third, “the bare point already obeys (mu)”, had never been measured: it fails on 2 of 60 as returned.

rows.caught_by: the Claude track, then an audit
rows.what: A reason given in one of our audit notes was wrong: it said only an R(7)-type premise forbids two equal common rows, but codegree 8 and 9 are impossible outright on 40 vertices. Its conclusion stood; no verdict changed.

mattered.title: Our own wrong reason
mattered.line: In box 3: our audit note said only an R(7)-type premise forbids two equal common rows. Codegree 8 and 9 are impossible outright on 40 vertices. The conclusion stood; an erratum was filed.

rows.how: an audit of the four-edge spec
rows.what: A slip in our own note (a size-three row described by its size instead of its zero type) was carried into a model’s spec.

rows.caught_by: an outside review I pasted in
rows.what: The two seals’ Bitcoin receipts were still pending in our records, hours after a block could confirm them.

rows.how: rereading Chen’s repository before a note to him
rows.what: Our result note (in its sealed text too), our reveal draft and our first note to Chen called R(7) Chen’s open case. His own AI run had excluded it first, on 21 Nov at 16:50:52 UTC.
rows.outcome: our wording changed: a second computation of a case his run closed first; the sealed sentence is corrected beside it, in box 2

mattered.title: Chen’s run had closed R(7) first
mattered.line: Found by our own reread of his repository before writing to him. Our wording changed to “a second computation”, and a sentence of our sealed note is corrected beside it.

rows.how: an audit of the four-edge catalogue plan
rows.what: A model’s estimate of 42 to 43 minutes to build the four-edge catalogue was not supported.

rows.how: an audit of the prose items
rows.what: Three wording slips in a model’s report on the three-edge branch’s prose items; no error in our programs.
A model’s reading called a lower bound “Chen’s”; it is an unnumbered lemma in an idea-scout note of his run, not in his claims list.
rows.outcome: the page names it as the scout note’s

rows.what: We read the three-edge registration’s timestamp receipt only in part (its listing cut after four lines) and “corrected” its Bitcoin time to 02:08 UTC on 23 November. The whole receipt holds three attestations, the earliest block 977085 at 18:17:27 UTC on 22 November.

rows.caught_by: the reveal day’s prior-art re-check (an agent)
rows.what: Our prior-art scout of 21 Nov missed a public note (andrey-kokoev/marici, dated 9 Nov) that had posed the induced-C35 question and left it not excluded.
rows.outcome: the page cites it beside the theorem

rows.caught_by: the reveal package (an agent), reading Chen’s history
rows.what: Our 04:02 note put the label “cert (custom trace)” of Chen’s C-004 at his round 1; it arrived in round 2, at 17:49:01 UTC.
rows.outcome: corrected in the reveal’s source and here

rows.whose: the second program (the Astra track’s code)
rows.how: a second program’s full run, joined with ours by our own code
rows.what: The second counting program, run over every core, disagreed with ours on 16 of the 10,425 cores then compared (32 of 23,409 in the end): it wrote more records after the Hall screen. Until each was decided, nothing about the box could say “all excluded”.
rows.outcome: resolved at 08:01 UTC; no verdict changes
rows.resolution: Resolved at 08:01 UTC: the second program was the one in error. It applied only the first of the Hall screen’s three side conditions, an omission inherited from its pilot version; ours applies all three. Across the catalogue: 32 cores, 14,895 extra records, every one refuted by our tests and found infeasible by our direct decider, so no verdict would change even if they were counted. The corrected version agrees with ours on 129 cores (a laptop) and on 6,512 (a rented run stopped on cost); it was never run on all 23,409.

rows.what: The four-edge cost pilot’s ENDED line was lost: our launch line sent its standard output to /dev/null after appending it to run.log, so run.log is empty. The pilot log, the room ledger and the summary are intact.

The registered cost of the four-edge branch, about US$2,530, was biased low: 9 of the 20 drawn cores were on the enumerator’s slow path, where 66.4% of the catalogue sits. Weighted by the catalogue: about US$3,111.
rows.outcome: the estimate replaced; the branch not run

rows.what: This ledger said the second program would be corrected and compared again over every input when the run ended. The corrected version was compared on 129 cores, then on 6,512 on a rented machine before that run was stopped on cost; never on all 23,409.
This ledger called the second program independent. Its counting path was written after its track had read and patched ours: separately written, not blind.

rows.how: reading a receipt that had never been upgraded
rows.what: The page said the rules of the R(7) run were timestamped before the pod existed. The stamp was submitted at 02:13 UTC, before the pod; Bitcoin confirms it only from block 976978 (02:48 UTC), 31 minutes after production began. The sealed box’s line had the same wording.
rows.outcome: both sentences reworded; the sealed record files keep the old words, with this line beside them

rows.how: reading the registration against the files
rows.what: Three steps registered for after the run had no record or not the registered form: the same programs on 12 cores on a second kind of machine, the machine’s own hash list, and a separate tally with its program kept.
rows.outcome: the 12-core recheck was then made, late: 12 of 12 equal (09:51 UTC, 24 Nov); the other two are listed in box 3

rows.how: reading the registration against the files
rows.what: The file of deviations lists one. The stop at 16,927 cores, the second machine and a start by hand were recorded in the log only.

rows.how: reading the record before it opened
rows.what: A derivation note in the record says “R(7), not yet closed”. Chen’s run had closed it the day before.
rows.outcome: corrected beside the file, in box 3

rows.what: Our log called the ledger’s hash (34a67324…5d7b) the hash of FINAL.sha256; it is the ledger’s line inside it. The file FINAL.sha256 itself, which the receipt commits to, hashes to e7769301…fb0a.

rows.how: ruling the gate by its own words
rows.what: A report called gate G4b a PASS. By the gate’s own terms it is a FAIL: the gate asked for a route with a finite projected total under 5,000 core-hours, and the report’s own first line says no complete argument has a defensible price.

rows.whose: a file of round 1 (the Claude track)
rows.what: A control file named exoo39.g6 has 172 edges; the class identified as Exoo’s graph has 167. Both are valid 39-vertex controls; the file’s name is not a claim that it is Exoo’s.

rows.how: an audit run over all 6,180 non-regular distributions
rows.what: Our roster of 519 non-regular distributions was built with Chen’s unchecked floors. Without them, one more key survives at the lower tier, (8,0,0,32); the hole closes at the higher tier.
rows.outcome: listed; the key later excluded by the three-lows theorem

rows.what: The one-level counting row at k = 8 was given as 30; with neighbours’ degrees per vertex the true row is 29.
An agent’s report gave 7 and 10 roots at (23,6); the numbers were 6 and 9.

rows.how: ruling the gate by its own words
rows.what: A report’s verdict line said “PASS UNIFORM” for an inequality whose weights can differ by host: that is the LP’s dual in one form, not one inequality. Part 3 of the gate was not met.
A control file called control167.g6 has 168 edges; the audited 167-edge graph was used for the reported control.
Two bugs in an auditor’s own search were caught by its completeness checks against a brute force, before the full run.

rows.how: reading the gate against the W1c table
rows.what: The W1i gate text said a pass would mean every involution type of the cap-3 window is decided. Wrong: the W1c table leaves 2^14 1^12 and the loopless case of 2^13 1^14 open, and no later certificate closes them.
rows.outcome: corrected in the ledger; the open types listed; the next gate (W1j) asks for those two
